A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the inverse scattering problem for a given partial channel has been solved in a general case of two-particle systems in terms of nonlocal potentials, which are defined by a given set of scattering data and by a given choice of the wave function.

we have found the solution of the general inverse scattering problem for two-body systems with arbitrary nonlocal potentials in the form of an explicit integral transform, which is a natural generalization of the Gelfand-Levitan-Marchenko equation.

the inverse scattering problem in the present approach is solved in the framework of the theory of generalized functions and the theory of distributions, with the latter theory being used as a mathematical language of quantum mechanics.
The main takeaway from our work is that

quantum mechanics is a theory of the probability distributions of quantum-mechanic systems, which is a generalization of classical mechanics, and that the quantum-mechanical description of the system is incomplete without the specification of the probability distributions.
the inverse scattering problem is not unique, and that the arbitrariness of the solution is related to the arbitrar-iness of the phase-equivalent nonlocally acting potentials.
the scattering data for the inverse scattering problem are not sufficient for a unique recovery of a quantum-mechanical system.
